Probate in Washington: What Actually Happens After a Parent Dies

8 min read·Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law

Your mother died eleven days ago. There is a will somewhere, a house with a mortgage, a bank that will not talk to you, and a sibling who has opinions. Somebody told you probate takes years and eats a third of the estate, which is true in some states and is not true here. Probate in Washington is one of the more efficient systems in the country, and understanding why will tell you a great deal about the next several months.

Is probate required in Washington?

Often it is not. No Washington statute compels you to open a probate. Whether you need one depends on what the decedent owned and how it was titled.

If everything passed outside probate, by community property agreement, beneficiary designation, payable-on-death account, survivorship, or a funded trust, there may be nothing for a probate to administer. If there is real property titled in the decedent's name alone, you will almost certainly need one, because no bank, buyer, or title company will accept a conveyance from someone with no authority to sign.

One obligation does not depend on opening a probate. RCW 11.20.010 requires the person holding the will to either deliver it to the named personal representative or file it with the court within thirty days of learning of the death, and a named personal representative has forty days to file it. Willful failure can create liability to anyone damaged by the delay. The will gets filed even when no probate follows.

The small estate affidavit

For modest estates there is an alternative to probate entirely. Under RCW 11.62.010, where the assets otherwise subject to probate are valued at less than $100,000 and include no interest in real property, a successor can claim the decedent's personal property by affidavit rather than through an estate administration.

Three limits define it. Only personal property transfers this way, so a single parcel of real estate takes the procedure off the table. Only a "successor" as defined in RCW 11.62.005(2) may use it, meaning a beneficiary under the will or by intestacy, or a surviving spouse or domestic partner as to their half of the community property; creditors cannot. And advance written notice to the other successors is required.

The bank that transfers in reliance on a valid affidavit is released from liability. The recipient is not. Under RCW 11.62.020 the claiming successor remains accountable to any personal representative later appointed.

Opening the estate and admitting the will

A probate is opened by petition in the superior court of the county where the decedent lived. In Spokane County that is Spokane County Superior Court. The court admits the will, appoints a personal representative, and issues letters testamentary, which is the document the bank will finally accept.

One misconception is worth correcting early: the eldest child is not automatically in charge. If there is a will, the person named in it has first claim to serve. If there is no will, RCW 11.28.120 sets the priority, running surviving spouse or registered domestic partner first, then children, then father or mother, then brothers or sisters, then grandchildren, then nephews or nieces. Birth order does not appear in the statute, and in every case the authority comes from a court appointment rather than family consensus.

Nonintervention powers, and why Washington probate is efficient

This is the feature that distinguishes Washington, and the reason the horror stories you have read do not describe what is about to happen to you.

A personal representative may petition for "nonintervention powers" under Chapter 11.68 RCW. RCW 11.68.011 sets two threshold conditions: the will must not specifically preclude them, and the estate must be solvent. If those are met, the court may grant the powers where the petitioner is the personal representative named in the will, or, in an intestate estate, where the petitioner is the surviving spouse or domestic partner, the estate consists solely of community property, and all of the decedent's reasonably identifiable living issue are also that spouse's issue. A petitioner outside those categories can still seek the powers after notice under RCW 11.68.041.

What the powers do is remove the court from the administration. Under RCW 11.68.090 a personal representative holding them may borrow money for the estate, lease or mortgage or encumber estate property, sell or exchange it, make interim distributions, and settle the estate, all without notice to the court and without a court order. The Supreme Court has put the consequence directly, holding that the superior court has no role in administering a nonintervention estate except in narrow, statutorily enumerated situations.

In a supervised probate every significant act requires a hearing. In a nonintervention probate, after appointment the personal representative administers much as a trustee would, and most estates never see a courtroom again.

Creditor claims, and the deadline that matters most

Notice to creditors is optional in Washington. The personal representative is not required to publish it. Publishing is usually the right call anyway, because it starts a short clock instead of a long one.

How long a creditor has depends entirely on what the personal representative did, and the four possibilities are set out in RCW 11.40.051:

Where notice was published and a reasonably ascertainable creditor received actual notice, the claim is barred on the later of thirty days from service or mailing of that notice or four months after first publication. RCW 11.40.051(1)(a).

Where notice was published and the creditor was not reasonably ascertainable, the claim is barred four months after first publication. RCW 11.40.051(1)(b)(i).

Where the creditor was reasonably ascertainable but received no actual notice, the claim is not barred until twenty-four months after the date of death. RCW 11.40.051(1)(b)(ii).

Where no notice was published at all, claims are barred twenty-four months after the date of death. RCW 11.40.051(1)(c).

Two refinements change how those periods actually operate. The claims statute shortens the time to come after an estate, but it does not extend any otherwise applicable statute of limitations. RCW 11.40.051(2). And claims satisfiable entirely from liability or casualty insurance proceeds sit outside these deadlines under RCW 11.40.060, which is why a car accident claim can surface long after you thought the estate was closed.

Inventory, accounting, distribution, and closing

The personal representative prepares an inventory and appraisement of estate assets as of the date of death under RCW 11.44.015. In a nonintervention estate it is not automatically filed, but any beneficiary, any unpaid creditor who has filed a claim, or the Department of Revenue may request a copy, and it must be furnished within ten days. RCW 11.44.015(2). Under RCW 11.44.035 a party in interest may challenge the inventory at any stage.

Closing is usually done by a declaration of completion under RCW 11.68.110 rather than by petitioning for a decree of distribution. A copy goes to each party who has not waived notice, with the statutory notice of filing. Those parties then have thirty days to ask the court to review the reasonableness of fees or to request an accounting. If nobody does, the personal representative's actions and fees are deemed approved and discharge is automatic.

Where this goes wrong

Distributing before the creditor period runs. This is the serious one. A personal representative who pays the beneficiaries early and then faces a valid claim has no estate left to pay it from and is looking at personal exposure. The related trap runs the other way: because notice to creditors is optional, a fiduciary who skips notice and thereby forces payment of a claim that publication would have barred can be personally liable for the difference. Both failures come from treating the creditor machinery as paperwork rather than as the thing that protects the person administering the estate.

Missing the nonclaim deadline from the creditor's side. If you are owed money by someone who died, the four-month window after first publication is short, strictly applied, and nobody is obligated to remind you.

Real property never conveyed out. This is among the most common problems in the practice area. A parent dies, the family divides things informally, nobody probates anything, and title to the house still stands in the name of someone who has been dead for decades. It stays invisible until somebody tries to sell or refinance, at which point it is a title defect that has to be cured under time pressure, with heirs who may be scattered or deceased themselves.

Treating the role as honorary. A personal representative is a fiduciary. Under RCW 11.28.250 a court may remove one for waste, embezzlement, mismanagement, fraud, incompetence, wrongful neglect, or any other necessary cause. RCW 11.68.070 extends removal or restriction to a nonintervention personal representative who fails to execute the trust faithfully, and lets a prevailing beneficiary recover attorney fees. The Supreme Court has confirmed the catch-all ground reaches a nonintervention personal representative too.

Why this is lawyer work

Most of a probate is judgment, not forms. Whether to petition for nonintervention powers, whether to publish notice to creditors and when, whether a particular asset is even part of the estate, whether a claim should be paid or rejected, how to handle a beneficiary who wants a distribution now against a creditor period with four weeks left. Those decisions carry personal consequences for the person serving, and they are made in sequence, where an early choice closes off later options. A probate also puts one family member in a fiduciary role over property siblings believe is partly theirs, at the worst possible moment emotionally, and having the deadlines calendared and the correspondence handled from outside the family prevents a meaningful number of the disputes that otherwise arrive six months in.

About my practice

I handle probate and estate administration from my office in downtown Spokane, and it is a substantial share of my practice. I represent personal representatives through nonintervention and supervised administrations, advise successors on whether a small estate affidavit will do the job, prepare and respond to creditor claims, clear title to real property never conveyed out of a prior estate, and litigate estate disputes when they arise. Spokane County probates proceed in Spokane County Superior Court, and I appear in the surrounding Inland Northwest counties as well.

Talk to me

If someone close to you has died and you are not sure whether a probate is necessary or who is supposed to be doing what, that is worth sorting out before decisions get made that are hard to undo. I offer a free initial consultation by appointment in downtown Spokane.
